Last winter, CoOpportunity Health, one of the 23 health care co-ops created by the ACA, went under after it could no longer afford to pay for the care of its customers, who turned out to be sicker than the co-op expected them to be. The co-op was one of the only insurers offering ACA plans in Iowa, and its collapse was a victory for big insurers. In the wake of its demise, it remains uncertain whether the company will be able to pay back federal loans of $147 million.

It now appears that CoOpportunity Health is not alone in the predicament it found itself. In case you missed it, the New York Times recently picked up on an audit released last month of the 23 co-ops created under the law. The story does not paint a pretty picture: 22 out of 23 co-ops lost money last year, and many could find it hard to repay the 2.4 billion that the federal government spent overall on the co-ops.

Lupus of Novae

St. Lupus from Novae (Sfântul Lup in Romanian) is a Dacian or Roman saint who was for a while the servant of St. Demetrius from Thessaloniki. The Romanian Orthodox Church reveres St. Lupus on August 23. Lupus lived in Novae, a Roman fortress in the Danube valley, today the Bulgarian town Svishtov.

St. Lupus lived at the end of the 3rd century and beginning of the 4th century, and was a faithful servant of the holy Great Martyr Demetrius of Thessaloniki (October 26). Lupus was present at the death of his master, and he soaked his own clothing with his blood and took a ring from his hand. With these objects St Lupus worked many miracles at Thessaloniki. He attacked pagan idols, for which he was subjected to persecution by the pagans, but he was preserved unharmed by the power of God. St Lupus voluntarily delivered himself into the hands of the torturers, and by order of the Emperor Galerius, he was beheaded by the sword on August 23, shortly after St. Demetrius death (probably in 307).

The old legion fortress of Novae turned into an Roman-Byzantine town in the 5th – 6th century . The ruins of the Bishop’s complex date back to those times. The ruins consist of a large basilica, residential houses with impressive baths, and a large building, which was designated for receiving the pilgrims to the local martyr St. Lupus. A baptistery impressive with its architecture was found west from the basilica entrance. It was an extension to the church in which Christianization was performed. Peter, the brother of the Emperor Mauricius (582-602) passed with his army through Novae at the end of the 6th century during his campaign in Dacian territories. A chronicle described the visit of Peter and the celebrations of St. Lupus day in Novae.

4K Video - is it worth it?

Yes.

Hell, 35mm film is equivalent to above 3K resolution. Have you ever seen a single movie? Your eyes are now ready for above 1080p.

*Another, much more detailed analysis.

Well there's different advantages, or lack of them, in 4k capture and production than there is in 4k display/playback and the advantages don't translate to all markets either. Cinema and TV playback aren't gonna see much advantage in displaying 4k, but will benefit from 4k production. Gaming and other visual oriented computing solutions will absolutely benefit from 4k display and rendering.

As a viewer, 4k won't make a difference to image integrity unless you're right up on the screen where with lower resolution images you would see pixelation (assuming 4k monitor and 4k content). That pretty much makes it pointless, from a solely viewing perspective, for your average cinema and TV applications where you typically are seated at a comfortable distance from the screen and pixelation isn't an issue. It's much the same argument as the great audiophile debate about high sample rate playback devices (like the Pono) which while there are technical advantages in the production arena, the delivery resolution of CD quality audio already surpasses the limits of human recognition.

However, increased resolution makes for increased detail, and hence realism, in production rendering so there are advantages for creating content in 4k, even if ultimately it is viewed at lower resolution. Help if possible, please! I downloaded a copy of Mint and installer to a USB stick, and after a few days in trial mode decided to install to laptop hard drive. Was asked how much of hard drive to partition for it and chose 100gb from 160gb on the drive. Unfortunately right at the end of the install a message said that it had failed. I can still boot up from Windows, and Mint using USB, but the partition I created causes an error message saying low on memory/storage. Can anyone tell me how to delete that partition so that I can have another attempt at a fresh install? Thanks in advance for any advice !

Assuming you have some computer skills, if not, then be extremely careful or let someone else do this.

In Windows:

  • Open Explorer (not Internet Explorer, but the files thingy)

  • Right-click on This PC (or This Computer)

  • Select Manage

  • Under Storage, select Disk Management

  • in the middle section in the bottom, find the drive

  • on that drive, click on the part that you want to delete (better make sure you have the correct one!)

  • right click on that part, select 'Delete Volume' (you still sure you have the right one?)

  • Select OK.

Now you can try to install Mint again to that empty space you just created.

No warranties here, if you delete the wrong partition you might be unable to start your computer or Windows ever again.

From here: http://forums.majorgeeks.com/showthread.php?t=220712

Windows - How To Make Partition Not Active:

Open up a command prompt and type DISKPART.

Type LIST DISK

Type SELECT DISK n (where n is the number of the active disk you wish to make inactive)

Type LIST PARTITION

Type SELECT PARTITION n (where n is the number of the active partition you wish to make inactive)

Type INACTIVE

Type EXIT to exit DISKPART

Type EXIT again to exit the command prompt

Reboot

You might have to go into Windows Power Shell and clean it up with DISKPART and create new volume and reformat. DISKPART help is pretty good. If you are computer literate you should have no problem figuring it out.
